claim: The reviewed seismic record classifies the source as a glacial collapse and debris flow from seismic and satellite evidence.
The agency event page reports that the collapse developed into a channelized debris-laden flood.
The reviewed source classification does not identify the perturbation that initiated the collapse.
No event-specific climate attribution can yet be assigned from the agency reconstruction.
Seismic timing, satellite mapping, and flow reconstruction indicate that rock and glacier ice failed together and transformed into a highly mobile debris flow.
Mapping and reconstruction indicate that the flood cascade did not require a glacial-lake outburst.
Snow and ice loading on the headwall and a preceding positive temperature anomaly were proposed as possible final perturbations.
The published hypotheses do not isolate a unique immediate trigger from structural release and progressive damage.
Long-term warming may have perturbed permafrost bedrock and promoted glacier decline and meltwater infiltration, but formal anthropogenic event attribution was not performed.
Surge-like stress enhancement and reduced basal friction allowed the frozen tongue's resisting forces to be exceeded.

About 10--25 mm of precipitation fell during the two days before failure and may have supplied liquid water, but causation was not established.
The event literature does not resolve a distinct short-term perturbation for the two-pulse Aru-2 collapse.
Increasing melt and rain over the preceding five to six years were inferred to raise subglacial water pressure in weak fine-grained till.

A rockslide struck and entrained a gully glacier before entering the fjord and generating a tsunami and very-long-period signal.
Wave and seismic modeling identified a cross-fjord seiche as the source of the nine-day very-long-period signal.
Sparse SWOT altimetry later observed water-level variations consistent in period and phase with the seiche reconstruction.
No meteorological, seismic, or other proximate trigger was demonstrated for 16 September 2023.
Multidecadal glacier thinning likely debuttressed the unstable toe; this is a mechanistic climate link rather than formal event attribution, and site-specific permafrost thaw was not shown.
The commonly used 2024 label is the paper's publication year; the landslide occurred on 16 September 2023.
A smaller rock or ice avalanche in the same gully likely generated the 11 October tsunami and week-long signal, but no new scar was resolved.
The source and proximate perturbation of the dependent October episode remain unresolved.
The October episode is not an independent event-level climate-attribution unit.
A bedrock landslide entered the fjord beside South Sawyer Glacier, generated a tsunami, and produced a globally detected seismic signal lasting as long as 36 hours.
Wave and seismic analysis identifies a fjord seiche as the source of the long-period signal.
Several days of rain were not extreme; the study did not isolate a unique immediate trigger.
Regional summer warming since 1875 was quantitatively attributed to anthropogenic forcing.
Observed retreat of South Sawyer Glacier supports glacier debuttressing as a preconditioning mechanism, but glacier retreat itself was not assigned an anthropogenic counterfactual fraction.
Several days of microseismicity accelerated in rate and magnitude until about one hour before failure.
Barry Arm is a monitored moving slope rather than an occurred catastrophic failure.
Slope acceleration was temporally coincident with glacier retreat, consistent with debuttressing; the reported cumulative-series correlation alone is not a causal test.
A possible precipitation response in 2017 was tenuous and did not persist in later observations.
